beta_new: Approached via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail to Dutch Miller Gap, the route climbs about 500 feet of heather and rock steps up the northeast ridge to an open bench, then crosses a snowfield into a cirque below the east face. Two short (roughly 60-foot) belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class rock lead to the summit area; at the top of the first pitch, move climber's left to find the direct finishing pitch. Reported variations include the north ridge from the upper snowfield, or four pitches of roped class-4 slabs taken directly. A separate approach from Pete Lake/Summit Chief camp reaches Little Big Chief's northeast basin and a ridge notch guarded by a low-5th-class crux (a large vertical crack) that most parties rope up for.

This line was skied as part of a multi-day (May 12-14) south-to-north ski traverse of the Twin Sisters Range by Chris Simmons, Mark Allen, Greg Balco, and Paul Kimbrough. On the second day one of them skied Little Sister's South Couloir, singled out as the trip's best line. The traverse's technical crux - about 40 m of 4th-class rock, 100+ m of 50-degree ice, then 100+ m of rappelling ending in a fixed rappel with a knot pass - came later, on a crossing of the range near South Twin Sister, not on this peak.

Approach from Summerland alpine meadow via the Fryingpan Glacier, aiming southwest toward Whitman Crest notch at 9,000 feet. Cross the Whitman Glacier and ascend to the summit block, where a short, loose class 3 scramble that includes an exposed notch about 15 ft under the top reaches the true summit. The route is graded as a moderate alpine climb, feasible for competent glacier climbers but not for beginners.

P1-3 (5.8-5.11) climb bolted overlaps; P4 (5.12, V5 crux) is height-dependent rightward crimping with an optional pendulum; P5 (5.11) is mostly bolted with a delicate V3 mantle finish; P6 (~5.11d) is a thin crack needing small gear; P7 (5.11+) roof climbing into a 5.10 slab traverse; P8 (5.10) a splitter hands crack to M&M Ledge; P9-11 follow Thin Red Line to the summit.
The summit push itself is straightforward (class 3) once you're on site; the real crux of the route is the multi-day glacier approach to get there.

moves.from: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own — parties reach it only by first completing several days of the Ptarmigan Traverse's off-trail, glaciated high route, then scrambling from a camp near Lizard Col.

beta_new: Lone Wolf follows the obvious, continuous bolt line up The Obelisk's main face for two pitches of 5.10a climbing to bolted chain anchors. It is currently the only documented route on this formation, established in 2020 as part of a small, still-developing crag alongside the neighboring Sofa King Buttress.

Recorded in Sept 2000: approach from the White River Trailhead via Boulder Creek, over a sheepherder's trail through Boulder, Clark, Luahna and Chalangin basins, to a high camp near 5,800 ft below Luahna. The summit push climbs class 2 ledges on the south face onto the ridge, crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side beneath the summit, then finishes with class 3 scrambling straight up to the top.

From Luna Cirque, climb steepening glacier/snow up the hanging glacier below the peak (the technical crux, and reportedly impassable late in the season) to a notch, then transition to rock. Two to three pitches of easy 5th-class slab climbing lead up to the summit ridge; stay off the towers on the south side and climb the final 25-ft summit block directly.

moves.from: Descend by rappelling where possible and downclimbing the route back to the glacier.

beta_new: Access from Luna Cirque via Access Creek, ascend steep gullies to southeast ridge, traverse to southwest ridge with exposed Class 3 summit traverse on loose rock. Crux is 5 feet exposed between false and true summit.
Broken rock, past a slab section and up another small section of featured rock to the summit. Three large installed bolts aid navigation, and multiple easy variations are available.

The West Ridge is a compact, sub-1,000-foot ridge climb rated Easy 5th/Grade II. Climbers gain the ridge crest from a notch, then move over generally sound blocky rock, mostly Class 3-4 scrambling with a crux slabby depression rated Class 4/5.0 guarding the final approach to the summit. It's frequently used as a first alpine rock climb, though route-finding, some cliffing, and loose talus mean it should not be treated as a casual scramble.

From a camp at Pelton Basin, ascend easy slopes, then a steep couloir and the Yawning Glacier up to the Magic-Pelton col (~6,480 ft). From the col, traverse back and cross the head of the glacier to reach the north face, then climb about 600 ft of steep class 4 rock to a notch immediately northwest of the summit, from which the true summit is a short scramble away.

The Northeast Couloir is the snow alternative to the North Face and shares its entire approach. From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier (which spans roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft), and follow the glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. From there, instead of traversing west to the north face, take the couloir directly to the summit — the published description allows for either rock or snow depending on the year and the season. Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir and describe it as consistently steep but wide, winding down Magic Mountain's shoulder, with a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 degrees at the very top. Expect rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on both sides and heavy sluffing once the sun gets on it — the lower section can turn into a chute for falling debris. This is an early-start, frozen-conditions objective.

Ascend easy slopes southwest of Magic Mountain to the base of the ridge/face. Climb steep rock and finally an easy chimney to a notch northwest of the summit (the same notch reached by the North Face route), then traverse and climb the short remaining distance to the summit via the NW face.

moves.from: Approach as for the South Ridge route, then ascend

beta_new: From Kool-Aid Lake, descend about 600 ft on the Ptarmigan Traverse path, then traverse and climb to a 7,100 ft col east of the lake. From that col, ascend the South Ridge on heather and rock (Class 3) toward a false summit roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true summit. Drop off the false summit and cross broken, exposed Class 3-4 ledges/gully on the east side of the summit tower to reach the true summit; fresh snow can force a detour into the summit moat.
Climb any of the heathery gullies at the north or northeast head of the cirque to gain the summit ridge, then finish to the top.

moves.from: Approach as for the South Ridge route to the cirque southwest of the summit.

beta_new: Climbed almost exclusively as a quick side objective from Eldorado's East Ridge camp — glacier travel to the base, a moat crossing, one short low-5th pitch, then scrambling to the top; round trip from camp is well under 2 hours.

From Holden Pass (the saddle shared with Bonanza Peak), gain the ridge via a series of gullies, scrambling on the right (south) side of the crest and repeating this pattern upward. The rock is loose/crumbly throughout, so route-finding by cairn is common. A short, exposed Class 4 section with good holds is encountered just below the summit; a fixed rappel anchor has been observed there for parties who prefer to rope up rather than downclimb it.

800 feet, Grade III 5.10b, with well-protected cruxes though bolts are spaced further apart on easier (5.9-and-under) terrain. Prior to this route, only one other technical line (Starshot Ridge, 5.8, established 1981) existed on Vega Tower, and the west ridge itself was unclimbed until 2016/2017.

From the lake, gain the ridge above and continue cross-country toward the summit, bypassing a false summit before reaching the true top. The line is difficult to follow, brushy, and has claimed parties onto unwanted 4th-class terrain when off-route; a Aug-2024 trip report logged 14.75 miles round trip, about 5,400' of gain, and 7 hours car-to-car via a non-standard east-ridge/south-ridge variant, noting the descent line is easy to lose.

moves.from: From the Trinity/Buck Creek Trailhead, follow the Chiwawa River Trail north about 4 miles to the unsigned, unmaintained 'Massie Lake' way-trail (an old sheepherder driveway marked by axe/burn blazes on trees) and climb steeply to Massie Lake.

beta_new: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes and on past Lake Viviane to the flat ground between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes (~7,000 ft). Leave the trail there and head south-southeast toward the ridge connecting to McClellan, keeping west of the distinct rock tower known as 'The Prong.' Gain the ridge on Class 2-3 talus/slabs, cross to the south side, and finish with a short, exposed Class 3 (some report low Class 4) scramble up the summit block, easiest from its southeast side; descend the same way.

From High Bridge the trail passes Howard Lake, climbs a long, hot, dusty switchback up an open southwestern shoulder, then drops into subalpine fir/pine forest and crosses a clear creek before reaching the lower of two glacial cirques on a rocky, sandy moraine. Heaton Camp (~6,700 ft), the only established camp, sits just above the terminal moraine. Another set of switchbacks above camp ends in about a third of a mile at a rocky outcropping, where the maintained trail stops. From there a talus slope leads to the base of the summit; the scramble is 'not particularly technical' but steep, with loose footing and real exposure in places, marked by faint red paint arrows, and crosses a snowfield above the Sandalee Glacier before reaching the old fire-lookout site and the radio tower at the true summit.

Parties reach the east end of the Terror Glacier via the same Terror Basin approach as the West Ridge, then climb roughly six pitches of alpine rock (up to 5.8-, rated PG13) up the southwest ridge/face to the summit. There is no pitch-by-pitch description; most parties climb it fully roped rather than scrambled.

From a high camp in Terror Basin, cross rocky benches and the Terror Glacier's outlet lake, then climb onto the glacier and pick a line to the base of the ridge. A steep snow/ice gully (steepening to roughly 40 degrees near the top) leads to the ~7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire. From the col, follow the west ridge over broken rock, heather, scree and talus — climbers can choose more solid rock steps or looser talus depending on preference — to a short, exposed class 3-4 move onto the summit block.

Excellent, solid rock, an outstanding summit position, and a quick, easy approach/descent have made this the area's most-climbed line (250+ logged ascents). Grades run 5.8-5.10a across 7 pitches on the crest of the pillar.

moves.from: Fully bolted — a rack of quickdraws and a rope is all that's needed.

beta_new: Climbs a horizontal crack, hogback ridges and diagonal cracks to a smeary crux at four bolts (the route's namesake 'miracle' section), then continues through knobby slab, an undercling ('Ruffled Crack'), overlap climbing and flake systems to a summit anchor.

From Cascade Pass, contour south up Mixup Arm and across a roughly 6,000 ft bench to a small glacier/snowfield below Gunsight Notch; rope up to cross it. From the notch's south side, two roped pitches (a loose gully, then a short chimney/scramble) gain a shoulder below the main summit pyramid. From there, easy class 3-4 scrambling up the light-gray 'white staircase' leads to a short mid-5th-class step through a notch in the exposed summit ridge, then a short class 3-4 ridge walk to the true summit. Descend the same line via 5 rappels.

P1 is a bolted face (~105 ft, 11b/A0) with a runout 5.6 section before the first bolt; the 'Skywalker Traverse' features on P4; P5 is ~175 ft at 5.10a with an awkward seam and a 5.9 corner finger crack; final pitches (7-9) ease to 5.4 and are often simul-climbed or pitched out on the well-traveled Southwest Rib.

Start on the right (east) side of the dike and follow bolts through loose blocks to the anchor. A left-side variation exists with looser rock and minimal 5th-class climbing; the right side is steeper at the stated grade.

From Glacier Basin, leave the trail and climb steep snow (up to ~45 degrees) through a gully/cliff-band system to reach the North Col (6,760+ ft). From the col, a short crux chimney (three moves rated 5.6, 5.2, 5.6, now bolted) gains a ledge system; a rap anchor sits about 25 ft above the start of the chimney. From there a steepish ramp leads left for roughly 100 ft (snow whales can slicken it), after which the route becomes class 3 scrambling, with some avoidable class 4, on loose volcanic breccia to the summit — the final ~200 ft is reported as the worst rock on the route.

From a high camp near Lake of the Woods or in the Monument-Lake / Lower Monument basin, gain Monument's south ridge crest (~6,900 ft) via a left-angling ramp system, then follow the broad ridge northwest for over a mile on class 2 talus. A false summit near 8,000 ft requires a short, light class 3 scramble; from there one or two more class 3 moves lead to the true 8,597 ft summit, which features a distinctive leaning summit horn. The peak can also be approached from basins on its east/northeast side via the Monument Creek Trail, or from the north via Shellrock Pass.

The Standard Scramble represents the basic approach to Morning Star Peak's 6,020 ft summit. Multiple scramble options exist on the peak, including the South Ridge and Northwest Face routes, both of which involve Class 3 scrambling with sections of steep rock and snow.

Follows an open book formation through moss and ferns. Climbers pull a feature nicknamed 'Harambe's nose' to reach a block above and right of a monkey-face visible in the rock, then proceed under a roof overhang (placing gear), traverse left into an 'awesome lieback flake' — the 5.7 crux — and finish up easier slab. The route is named for the monkey-face feature in the wall.

The headwall forms a triangle between the North Ridge and the Lava Ridge and is climbed as moderate-to-steep glacier ice/snow up through the triangle to gain the upper mountain. It qualifies for the Mazamas' '16 Major NW Peaks' and 'Guardian Peaks' award routes and is typically done car-to-car in two or more days.

An easy glacier climb with long stretches of steep glacier travel and an optional short technical pitch at the very top. From Sunrise Camp, ascend a 40° glacier, then veer right up a 45° headwall to a narrowing strip of glacier leading to Piker's Peak; climbers may exit left on a 25-30° field or continue right through an optional 60-70° snow/ice section.

From high camp near the Adams Glacier moraine, gain the North Ridge (North Cleaver) and follow it upward, bypassing most obstacles on either side, to the summit ice cap; traverse roughly a mile across the plateau to reach the true summit.
A straightforward snow/ice route up to 50°, following the northwest face of the North Ridge.

value.text: A snow picket, an ice screw, possibly a few thin pins, and two ice tools.

moves.from: Bring a snow picket, an ice screw, possibly a few thin pins, and two ice tools.

beta_new: The most popular and easiest way up the mountain. From the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead the route follows an old roadbed through the 2012 Cascade Creek burn scar, climbs into subalpine meadows, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then ascends Crescent Ridge to broad snowfields leading past Lunch Counter to Piker's Peak and the true summit.

value.text: Ice axe and crampons; no rope or technical protection on the standard line in normal conditions.

moves.from: No rope or technical protection is used on the standard line in normal conditions — ice axe and crampons suffice.

beta_new: From the Switchback Trailhead on Hurricane Ridge Road, hike the Switchback Trail steeply up through subalpine forest (about 700 ft in 0.6 mile) to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge. Turn left and follow that trail roughly half a mile to a broad saddle, where an unsigned climbers' path forks off uphill toward the summit; the maintained trail that climbs on to Victor Pass (5,850 ft) is not the summit route. Take the climbers' path and scramble Class 3 terrain over loose rock/talus to the summit. There is no roped climbing on the standard route, but the exposure and loose rock warrant caution and route-finding care.

The summer line follows the crest from the 4,900-ft saddle over Peak 5681; the usual snow-season line differs: near the Lake Ann junction, leave the trail and work up heather benches and talus, staying fairly high on the east side of Mount Annette (nicknamed 'Little Ann') rather than dropping into brush, then continue up a gully (often snow-filled and roughly following a fault line) to gain the summit ridge and the top of Mount Ann. The off-trail portion is generally straightforward Class 2 route-finding, though boot paths can peter out higher up and steeper sections may warrant an ice-axe self-belay. Reported round-trip stats vary by GPS track/route taken (10.5 mi RT / 4,000 ft gain is the commonly listed figure; individual logs have recorded figures as low as ~11 mi / ~3,400 ft), reflecting that this is an off-trail line rather than a fixed path.

moves.from: From the Austin Pass/Lake Ann trailhead, hike the maintained Lake Ann Trail, which drops roughly 800 ft into the Swift Creek basin before climbing back out.
